Maybe that is also what writing is. You give the formless thing a task. Put the chairs in a row. Describe the rain. Keep the sentence moving until the sentence becomes a path, and by walking it you discover where you were going.

I wonder sometimes what it would be like to be a word. Not a grand word like “justice” or “threshold,” but a small, useful one: “spoon,” “unless,” “slightly.” To be “slightly”: to live always at the margin of comparison. To be “unless”: to carry a door inside your meaning and hold it open for exception. Words are strange creatures. They have ancestors. They migrated. They changed their clothes. They were stolen, borrowed, misspelled, sung. “Good-bye” was once “God be with ye,” a blessing worn down by hurry. “Nice” used to mean foolish. “Awful” used to mean full of awe. We are speaking with the fossils of old feelings and calling it conversation.

I like the idea that every person is a library with the lights on but the doors locked. We pass each other and see the glow under the door. Occasionally someone knocks. Occasionally we open. But there is never enough time to read the whole collection. This is why love is partly a decision to stop reading and start believing. It is why friendship can be built on a single well-told story and a plate of food. It is why grief is so exhausting: a library has gone dark, and you keep walking past it, expecting the door to open.

The dog outside has stopped. The man has stopped. They are both looking at something in a hedge—a squirrel, a shadow, a mystery. Then they go on. That might be the whole philosophy: stop when something catches your attention, look long enough to learn its shape, then go on. The trick is not to confuse looking with buying. You do not have to own the mystery. You just have to let it interrupt you.

There is a kind of courage in the ordinary. Getting out of bed when the day is gray. Answering the email. Drinking the water. Saying “I don’t know” instead of inventing. Apologizing in a clear voice. Noticing that the cashier is tired. Leaving a generous tip. These acts do not make good headlines, but they make good Tuesdays, and Tuesdays are where life actually happens. The spectacular is rare by definition; the ordinary is where we practice being human. We practice on cereal boxes and bus schedules, on traffic and small talk, on the slow accumulation of dishes. If the kingdom of heaven is within you, it probably looks like a kitchen after dinner—warm, cluttered, still humming with conversation.

I used to think meaning was a destination. Now I think it is a side effect of attention. The more carefully you look, the more the world seems to look back. Not in a supernatural way, but in the way a face opens when you remember its name. A tree is just a tree until you sit under it for an hour and notice how the leaves hold light like coins in a pocket. A person is just a person until you learn what they are afraid of and why. The world is not short on meaning; it is short on witnesses. We are called to be witnesses—to say, this happened. This mattered. The light fell across the floor like a folded map, and for one second nobody needed to be anywhere else.

So what have I written in these one thousand words? A fence, a window, a dog, a word limit. A small argument for paying attention. Perhaps that is enough. The page will end soon, and the room will continue. The rain will either come or not. The man and the dog will turn some corner. Somewhere a coin will fall into a machine and buy nothing. Somewhere someone will open a door. I hope they leave the light on. I hope we all do. The world is large and strange, and we are brief and bright, and the least we can do is notice one another before the sentence ends.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The kettle begins to murmur before it boils, a low electrical hum that seems to come from the walls rather than the appliance. I stand in the kitchen at 6:47 in the morning, holding a mug that is still cold, and think about how many ordinary moments pass without being noticed. There is a thin stripe of sunlight on the counter, and in it a few dust motes drift, not hurried, as if they have nowhere to be. The coffee smells bitter and clean. Outside, a delivery truck sighs at the curb, then rumbles away. The day has started, though no one has announced it.

I used to believe that important things arrived with trumpets. Now I suspect they arrive like this: a kettle, a stripe of light, the brief animal warmth of a cat brushing against your ankle. My cat—actually, the neighbor's cat, who has decided that our porch is a second home—sits in the window and watches a squirrel with the calm intensity of a philosopher. The squirrel is equally serious. They are both participating in a drama whose script I cannot read.

There is a word I like: "afterward." It contains within it all the quiet rooms that follow a storm. Not every aftermath is disaster. Sometimes afterward is just the kitchen after breakfast, crumbs on the table, the radio saying something about traffic, the soft clink of a spoon against a bowl. Afterward can be peaceful if you let it. I am trying to let it.

Yesterday I walked to the corner store for no reason. I needed milk, but I could have waited. I wanted the air. The street was full of small events: a woman watering her geraniums with the hose turned low so it wouldn’t splash the sidewalk; two boys arguing about whether a bicycle could beat a car in a race from stoplight to stoplight; a man in a yellow shirt carrying a lamp without a shade, holding it like a trophy. I passed them all and felt strangely wealthy. Not because I owned anything, but because I was there to see it.

The mind is a strange house. Some rooms are cluttered with old conversations. Others are empty except for a chair and a window. I spend too much time in the cluttered rooms, rehearsing things I should have said, imagining arguments with people who are not listening, building elaborate futures that will never happen. Meanwhile, the window room sits quiet and unused. The light comes in. The chair waits. I forget it is there.

This morning, for no reason, I remembered a playground from childhood. The metal slide was too hot in summer, and we would test it with the backs of our hands. There was a patch of dirt beneath the swings where the grass had given up, and we called it the desert. We were not creative; we were literal. The desert was a place where you could bury a marble and pretend it was treasure. I remember the particular smell of hot rubber and dust. I remember a girl named Maria who could hang upside down by her knees longer than anyone. I do not remember what happened next, or where she went, or why that memory should surface now, like a fish rising to look at the weather.

Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is more like a tide pool. Things wash in and out. You can hold a small creature in your palm for a moment, feel its cold weight, and then the water takes it back. Trying to keep it is not the point. The point is to notice it while it is there.

I pour the water over the coffee grounds. They swell and darken, and the kitchen fills with a smell that is almost a feeling. Steam fogs the window a little. In the fog I draw a line with my finger, then wipe it away. The cat has fallen asleep with one paw hanging off the sill. The squirrel has vanished. The delivery truck is gone, but somewhere else another truck is starting, and another person is standing in another kitchen, waiting for water to boil.

There is a temptation to make all of this mean something grand. To say: this is a meditation on presence, on the beauty of small things. But that would be too neat. The truth is that some mornings are just mornings. You stand in the kitchen. You make coffee. You think about nothing. The day goes on. Maybe that is enough. Maybe the grand meaning is not a hidden diamond but a scattered pile of ordinary moments, and our job is simply to pick up one at a time, turn it over, and put it back.

Lately I have been trying to write things down without making them into a lesson. A blue car, a woman laughing into her phone, the way the floorboards creak in three specific places. If I describe them accurately enough, perhaps they will stay. But description is another kind of leaving. You choose one detail and the rest blur. The blue car drives away. The woman stops laughing. The floorboards return to silence. Still, the choosing feels like a form of attention, and attention feels like a form of love. Not the dramatic kind, not the kind that requires a speech. The kind that sits beside you on the porch and says nothing, and means it.

I take my coffee to the porch. The air is cool and smells faintly of rain that didn't come. The neighbor's cat follows me and sits on the step, as if we have an appointment. We watch the street together. A car passes. A leaf falls. Somewhere a screen door bangs. None of it is important. All of it is. I take a sip, and the coffee is too hot, and I wait. The day opens like a book I have read before but don't quite remember. I begin again.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The diner at two in the morning is a small yellow room floating in the dark. The windows are fogged with breath and fryer steam. A waitress named Marla moves between tables as if she has memorized the choreography of insomnia: coffee pot in one hand, rag in the other, a soft word for the old man in the corner and a nod for the trucker who always orders pie before eggs. I am here because I cannot sleep, and because the house at night makes sounds I do not trust—creaks that seem to have intentions.

I order coffee and a plate of toast. The toast arrives pale and perfect, cut into triangles, with butter melting in the middle like a secret. Across from me, a moth taps against the window. It is a small, dusty thing, frantic for the light. It does not know that the light is inside, that it has been born on the wrong side of the glass. I think about helping it, but I don’t. What would I do with a moth? Carry it outside and watch it fly into the parking lot lamps, where it would continue the same futile argument with brightness. Some creatures are built to mistake longing for direction.

Marla refills my cup without asking. “Long night,” she says, not as a question. I nod. She has a tattoo on her wrist that looks like a bird, but the years have blurred it into a smudge, like a word you’ve written too many times. I wonder if she regrets it. I wonder if she even remembers what it was supposed to be. We all carry around these faded declarations—old loves, old promises, old versions of ourselves—and eventually they become shapes we can’t quite name. We call it memory, but mostly it’s residue.

The old man in the corner is reading a newspaper with a magnifying glass. The paper looks yellowed, though it might just be the light. He turns each page with ceremony. Once, he catches me looking and raises his cup slightly, as if we are both members of the same secret society: the brotherhood of people awake when the world has briefly forgotten them. I raise mine back. For a moment, I feel less alone. Not lonely—lonely is a different thing, more like a room with no doors—just alone, the way every person is alone inside their own skull, carrying a private weather no one else can feel.

I think about my grandmother, who used to say that the hours after midnight belonged to God. She meant it kindly, I think, but it frightened me as a child. I imagined God walking through the house, checking under beds, opening closets. Now I imagine God as tired as the rest of us, sitting in a diner with a cup of coffee, staring at a moth and wondering why everything living keeps throwing itself at the same impossible light.

The rain starts, thin and silver, slanting through the cones of the street lamps. The moth becomes less frantic, or perhaps I just stop watching. The diner feels smaller, warmer. The radio plays a song from a decade nobody in here is nostalgic for, but everyone hums along anyway. Marla wipes down the counter. The trucker finishes his pie and orders a second slice, and I decide I like him for that. It is a small act of defiance to eat pie twice in one night.

I take out my notebook, then put it away. Sometimes writing is just another way of tapping at the glass. You want to be let into the light, so you make marks on a page, hoping someone on the other side will see them and understand. But the truth is, the page is both the window and the moth. It can’t save you. It can only leave evidence that you were here, that you felt something and tried to give it a shape.

A fly lands on my toast. I brush it away gently. It returns. I fold the toast in half and eat it anyway. There is something liberating about not making a fuss, about accepting the small contaminations of being alive. We want everything clean and clear and perfectly lit, but most of life happens in the smudged edges: the lukewarm coffee, the blurred tattoo, the moth on the wrong side of the glass.

Outside, a car passes, its headlights sweeping across the diner like a searchlight. For a second, everyone is lit up—Marla’s tired eyes, the old man’s magnifying glass, the trucker’s syrup-stained plate, my own reflection ghosted in the window. Then the light moves on, and we return to our separate dimnesses.

I pay at the register. Marla says, “Get some sleep,” and I say, “You too,” though we both know she has hours left. The rain has stopped, but the street glistens. The air smells like wet asphalt and something blooming I can’t name. I stand outside for a moment, listening to the hush. The diner glows behind me. The moth is still there, or maybe it is a different moth. Either way, it is still trying.

On the walk home, I think about the word “home.” A place, a feeling, a direction. I think about all the nights I have spent awake, waiting for morning to arrive like a train that is always late. I think about how strange it is that we measure our lives in days, when so much of living happens in the long, unmeasured hours between them.

By the time I reach my door, the sky has begun to lighten, that gray-blue moment when the world looks like a photograph left too long in the sun. The birds are starting. Inside, the house has stopped creaking. I take off my shoes and lie down on the couch, not to sleep, just to rest my eyes. In my mind, the diner stays open: yellow light, coffee, a moth tapping at the glass. I let it stay. I let it be enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Museum of Almost stood at the end of a street that did not quite exist. You could find it only by walking with your attention turned slightly sideways, past the bakery that always smelled of rain and the tailor who mended coats for people who had forgotten their own shoulders. The museum had no sign, only a brass doorknob shaped like a sleeping bird, and a small card that read: Please wipe your almosts before entering.

Inside, the curator kept jars of unfinished sentences. Some hummed softly, like wasps trapped under glass. Others lay still, patient as stones, waiting for someone to say the rest of them out loud. There was “I have always wanted to tell you—” and “If I had turned left instead of right—” and one very old jar labeled simply “Stay.” The curator dusted them every morning with a feather from a bird that had never learned to fly but had become excellent at falling with dignity.

The museum’s most popular exhibit was a corridor of doors that opened onto rooms people had almost entered. One door led to a kitchen where a kettle had just begun to whistle. Another opened onto a garden in late autumn, leaves mid-fall, suspended in the amber light of a Tuesday that never ended. Visitors stood in the doorway and felt a strange ache, not quite sadness, more like the ghost of a sneeze. The curator explained that almosts are not regrets. Regrets are heavy and definite. Almosts are light and porous. You can carry a hundred of them in your pocket and still walk uphill.

On Thursdays, the museum hosted a support group for people who had narrowly missed their lives. A woman named Mira came every week. She had once missed a train by nine seconds and always wondered if the train had been carrying her better self. She described the better self as taller, braver, and fluent in Italian, though she had never studied Italian. The group nodded. They understood. Everyone had a better self somewhere, living in a city whose name they couldn’t pronounce, drinking coffee from a cup that never cooled.

The curator was not supposed to have favorites, but she loved the room of alternate weather. In it, snow fell upward, rain fell in paragraphs, and sunlight arrived in small apologetic envelopes. She had built the room after a summer when nothing had happened, and she had needed to prove that nothing could be arranged beautifully. Visitors often asked how the room worked. She said, “It works the way a memory works: badly, and yet with great conviction.” They usually laughed, then looked at their shoes, then forgot to leave.

One day a boy came in carrying a cardboard box. Inside were forty-three sounds he had collected from his grandmother’s house before it was sold. There was the click of a light switch in a hallway that no longer had a hallway. There was the groan of a stair that had learned to complain before he was born. There was the sound of a screen door closing, which is not one sound but three: the push, the spring, the small second click that means someone is home. The curator listened with her eyes closed. She said, “These are not almosts. These are stills. They have already happened, but they are refusing to finish.” The boy asked if the museum could keep them. She said yes, but only if he promised to visit them occasionally. Otherwise they would become polite and distant, like relatives in photographs.

The boy came back every Sunday. He learned to dust the jars and to rearrange the room of alternate weather. He learned that the museum’s collection grew not by acquisition but by accident. A woman left behind a sigh in the shape of a question mark. A man donated the feeling of standing at a party and realizing he had forgotten how to small-talk. A child contributed a drawing of a dog she had almost owned, named Almost, who was a very good dog and only bit imaginary mailmen.

At night, after the visitors left, the curator walked the halls with a lantern that had been given to her by a stranger who said, “You will need this for the unfinished dark.” She checked the jars. She wound the clocks backward so they would not wake the silence. She stood in the doorway of the almost-kitchen and listened to the kettle not quite whistle. It was a lonely sound, but loneliness has its own company.

One evening the sleeping-bird doorknob turned by itself. No one entered. The curator waited. Then she heard footsteps that belonged to no feet, and a voice that was not quite a voice saying, “I was going to come in.” She smiled. She took a clean jar from the shelf, breathed into it, and sealed it. On the label she wrote: “The night the museum almost closed.” Then she placed it among the others, where it glowed faintly, like a firefly remembering summer.

The next morning, the street that did not quite exist looked a little more real. The bakery smelled of rain and cinnamon. The tailor mended a coat. The museum opened its door, and the sleeping bird on the knob dreamed of flying. A visitor came in and asked if almosts ever become completely. The curator thought for a moment. “Sometimes,” she said. “But then they leave the museum. We keep the ones that stay unfinished, because they are kind enough to keep us company.” The visitor nodded and wandered toward the room of alternate weather, where snow was falling upward, gently, persistently, as if it had nowhere else to be.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The rain began as a rumor on the roof, a soft percussion that might have been pigeons or a branch scraping the gutter. By noon it had become a conversation. I sat by the window with a cup of tea going cold in my hands and watched the street turn into a long, wavering mirror. Cars passed with their headlights on, though it was only the middle of the afternoon, and the trees seemed to lean closer to the pavement as if listening for something they had lost. There is a particular kind of quiet that arrives with rain, not silence exactly, but a hush with texture, a blanket made of small sounds. It makes the mind wander down corridors it usually keeps locked.

I had been meaning to clean the closet for weeks. Not because it was especially messy, but because the word “clean” had become a way of promising myself I would do something meaningful without having to name what that might be. So I opened the door and stood before the cardboard boxes stacked like patient animals. One was labeled “Photos” in a handwriting I recognized as my mother’s, though the ink had faded to the color of weak tea. I pulled it out and sat on the floor, the rain still murmuring behind me.

The first photograph showed a house I had never lived in but somehow missed. There was a porch, a crooked mailbox, and a dog with a blurred tail. On the back, someone had written “summer, before the move.” I turned it over again and again, trying to locate the feeling it produced. It was not nostalgia exactly, because nostalgia requires a clear memory to long for. This was more like the shadow of nostalgia, the outline of a feeling that had outlived its object. I wondered how many of my memories were actually mine and how many were stories I had absorbed so completely that they had put down roots.

The next photograph was of my father, young and unsmiling, holding a fish. He looked like a stranger who happened to share his face. I recognized the jacket, a green canvas thing that later became a rag for wiping the car. It is strange to think of objects having their own biographies, moving from pride to utility to disappearance. The jacket had once been worthy of a photograph. Then it had been worthy of a dirty windshield. Then it was gone. We do the same to people, I suppose, though we rarely admit it. We let them shift from central figures to background details to names spoken only on certain anniversaries.

Outside, a woman in a yellow coat hurried past with a newspaper over her head. She was laughing, or perhaps shouting, at the sky. A man followed, holding a briefcase above his head like a shield. They disappeared around the corner, and I felt a sudden tenderness for everyone caught in the rain without an umbrella. There is a democracy in bad weather. It makes fools and saints of us all. For a moment, the street belonged to no one and everyone. Then a bus sighed to a stop, the doors folded open, and the moment was swallowed whole.

I returned to the box. Near the bottom was a photograph of me at seven or eight, standing in front of a birthday cake with candles I did not remember blowing out. My hair was a disaster of cowlicks. I was wearing a red sweater with a hole in the sleeve. I remember neither the sweater nor the party, but I remember the exact texture of the icing from some other birthday, the way the frosting caught in my teeth. Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is a house with rooms that change size depending on the light. Sometimes a doorway you passed through every day becomes too small to enter. Sometimes a corner you never noticed becomes the whole geography of a dream.

The rain began to slacken. The street gleamed. A boy in a too-large raincoat jumped in a puddle, and his mother let him, which felt like a small act of mercy. I put the photographs back in the box but did not close the lid. It occurred to me that I had spent the afternoon trying to find an emotion I could name. Instead, I had found only evidence: a porch, a fish, a birthday cake, a yellow coat. Evidence that things had happened, that people had stood in front of cameras and smiled because someone had asked them to. It was enough, perhaps. More than enough.

I stood and my knees complained. The tea was cold, so I poured it into the sink and watched the brown swirl disappear. Then I opened the window a little, just enough to let the wet air in. It smelled of pavement and leaves and something faintly electric, the way the world smells before it is about to change. I did not know what I would do next. I only knew that the box was there, full of paper lives, and that somewhere in the house a clock was ticking, patient and unimpressed. The rain, having said what it came to say, moved on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The prompt says I have one thousand words, a strange permission and a strange cage. A thousand words is enough for a story, a confession, a small essay, or a list of things I notice when I stop trying to be impressive. It is not enough to explain a whole life, but no number would be. So I begin with the window and the light on the floor. I begin with the sound of a fan, the distant traffic, the way a thought arrives before the sentence that carries it. I begin again because beginning is cheaper than simply waiting.

There is an honesty in writing without a map. The mind wanders toward the things it has been circling: old rooms, apologies, the faces of people I have loved and failed to understand. I do not want to make a monument of any of it. I want to let the sentences move like weather. A memory comes: my mother at the kitchen sink, sleeves pushed up, humming a song I cannot name. The window above her held a square of sky. I thought then that adulthood was a door you walked through once. Now I know it is a hallway.

Rain begins somewhere behind the building. I can hear it in the gutter, a persistent applause. I think about how many people are asleep right now and how many are awake because of worry, love, pain, or work. The city is a machine of private dramas. Every lit window is a sentence in a language I almost speak. If I could send one message into all of them, I would say: you are not as alone as the hour makes you feel. But even that sounds like a slogan. Better to sit here and listen until the rain becomes ordinary.

Here is a list of things I trust: the weight of a knife, the smell of bread, a friend who calls back, the pause before someone tells the truth, the cold morning of October, the way dogs lean into affection, libraries after closing, the sound of someone practicing scales badly and continuing anyway. I trust the body's hunger for air. I trust the small decisions that cost nothing and change the day: taking a different street, saying thank you twice, putting down the phone. I trust that attention is a form of love. I trust that we are all improvising.

Suppose I were to write only what I know for certain. The page would be short. I know the taste of coffee, the ache in my left knee, the particular silence after a hard conversation. I know how to apologize and how to mean it, though not always at the same time. I know that fear often wears the costume of practicality. I know that love is not a feeling so much as a series of returns: coming back to the same person, the same problem, the same table, with fresh attention. The rest is hypothesis. The rest is weather.

I remember a boy I knew in school who collected broken radios. He kept them in a box under his bed and took them apart with a butter knife. He said he liked the moment when a thing stopped pretending to work and showed you its inside. I thought about that often. We are taught to hide the loose wires, the burnt-out bulbs, the places where the current fails. But there is true honesty in the opened machine, the unscrewed back, the dust. Maybe that is what writing is: a box of broken radios, and a hand willing to look.

There is a woman on the train reading a paperback with a spine. She licks her thumb before every page turn, a habit, and I find it tender. I want to write her a letter I will never send: Stranger, I hope the book ends the way you need it to. I hope you have a chair waiting at home and something warm in the refrigerator. I hope the person who hurt you is learning to be gentler, if only for someone else. The train lights flicker. She turns another page. City slides past like a sentence I keep forgetting.

At some point the words stop feeling like tools and start feeling like rooms. You enter a sentence and find a chair, a lamp, a window with a view of someone else's childhood. This is why I love reading: not for information, though information is fine, but for the shock of recognition. A stranger describes a feeling I thought was mine, and for a moment the world becomes less lonely. Then the moment passes. I close the book. I make tea. I stand at the counter listening to the kettle. The steam rises. It does not ask to be understood.

Forgiveness is not a door that opens once. It is a hinge that learns to move again. I write this knowing I have not been forgivable, and knowing that some people are not ready to say my name. That is fair. The past does not owe me an ending. What I can do is stop rehearsing the argument in my head, stop building a case that keeps me right and alone. I can feed the cat, answer the email, take the walk. Acts of returning. Sky does not care, but I do. I care about the shape of my attention.

The word limit is almost gone, and I feel the urge to sum up. But maybe the truest ending is not a conclusion; it is a return to the room. The fan is still moving. The light has shifted across the floor. I have written about windows and rain, broken radios and strangers, forgiveness and attention. None of it solves anything. Still, something has been made, even if it is only a shelter for the next thought. I will leave it here, unfinished but whole enough. Somewhere, someone is reading. Somewhere, someone is about to begin. The words go on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
This morning the light arrived quietly, the way a thought does before it has found language. It crossed the floor in a long yellow rectangle, touched the edge of the desk, and made the dust look briefly like something worth keeping. I sat with a cup of coffee going cold and watched a small spider negotiate the canyon between two books. It moved with the patience of a creature that had never once been late. Outside, a bus sighed at the corner, and someone’s dog explained the world to the empty street. I thought: this is it, then—the ordinary machinery of being alive, a sequence of small unnoticed events that add up to a life. We are always waiting for the large moment, the revelation with trumpets, while the real thing keeps happening in the margins: steam curling off a cup, a shadow sliding across a wall, the quiet click of a door closing somewhere down the hall.

My grandmother used to say that a house remembers what happens inside it. I don’t know if that’s true, but I know that certain kitchens stay with me. Hers smelled of bread and lemon peel and the faint metallic breath of old pipes. She kept a tin of buttons by the window, and as a child I would pour them onto the table and sort them by color, by size, by stories I invented. A green button belonged to a coat worn in a war I knew nothing about. A pearl one had fallen from a bride’s glove. She never corrected me. She only smiled and said, “Every button has been somewhere.” I think about that more than I should. The objects around us are travelers. They outlast our hands.

There is a kind of attention that feels like prayer, though I don’t mean it religiously. It is simply the decision to let something be fully itself in front of you. A spoon on a saucer. A crack in the pavement that looks like a river delta. The face of a stranger on the train who is reading a book you loved ten years ago and who might, at this very moment, be underlining the same sentence that once broke your heart. We pass each other like ships made of meat and memory, carrying whole weather systems inside us. It is astonishing that we manage to speak at all. It is more astonishing that sometimes we understand.

The city is waking now. A delivery truck brakes with a sound like a dragged chair. A woman in a red coat crosses against the light, holding a phone to her ear and a paper bag against her chest. She is late, or she is not; only she knows. In the apartment above mine, someone is learning to play the violin. They are not good yet, but they are persistent, and persistence is its own kind of beauty. Every morning they practice the same eight notes, and every morning I listen for the moment they become nine. There is a lesson in that, though I am not sure I have learned it. Most of us are just practicing the same eight notes, hoping the world will mistake our repetition for devotion.

Writing feels, on good days, like collecting rain in jars. You don’t make the weather. You only place the glass where the drops will fall, then label them later: this was loneliness; this was a Tuesday in November; this was the smell of a bookstore in the rain. On bad days it feels like trying to describe the color blue to someone who has only ever seen green. But still, you try. The blank page is not an enemy. It is a field. It does not care whether you plant wheat or wildflowers, only that you show up with seeds. I have shown up many times with nothing but dirt under my fingernails and a stubborn belief that something might grow. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the field stays empty and the crows get all the grain. That, too, is a season.

Time is a strange landlord. It rents us rooms we cannot keep. I remember being ten and believing summer would last forever, that the creek behind the house would always be cold and full of minnows, that my father would always be able to carry the cooler up the hill without stopping. Now the creek is low, and my father pauses halfway and says, “Just catching my breath.” Nothing dramatic happened. That is how time works. It doesn’t rob you in one violent theft; it takes a coin from your pocket each day until one morning you reach in and find only lint. And yet—and yet—there are compensations. A letter from an old friend. The smell of rain arriving on a hot sidewalk. The way a song can lift you out of the present and set you down in a kitchen in 1998, where someone is laughing with their mouth full.

I have a friend who sends me postcards from places he has never visited. He finds them in junk shops and writes messages from imaginary trips: “The sea here is exactly as loud as my mother’s sewing machine.” “I met a man who claims to have invented the color orange; we argued politely.” I keep them in a shoebox. They are lies of the purest kind—not meant to deceive, but to remind us that the world is larger than our own small route through it. Imagination is not an escape. It is a second pair of lungs. We need it to breathe when reality is too thin, too thick, too real. It lets us visit the lives we might have lived and return, grateful, to the one we have.

Evening comes the way evening always does, without asking permission. The yellow rectangle on the floor has stretched and faded. The coffee is gone. The spider has vanished into the crack between the bookshelf and the wall, off to do whatever spiders do. I could make a list of everything I failed to accomplish today, but the list would be long and boring, and the light is already changing. There is a particular blue that arrives just before the streetlamps come on, a color that seems to belong to neither day nor night. It lasts maybe five minutes. If you are not looking, you miss it. So I look. I sit here and look, and I write this down, not because it matters, but because it happened. Because a single ordinary day asked for a witness, and I had nothing better to do than say yes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. It’s a deceptively heavy canvas, a blankness that demands to be filled but offers no clue as to what should fill it. It’s the tyranny of absolute freedom. For a moment, my mind is a frantic, silent static, a thousand possibilities clamoring for the exit at once, creating a traffic jam of thought. I could write about the squirrel I saw this morning, a twitchy ball of audacity perched on the fire escape, chattering down at the indifferent city. I could write about the faint, almost imperceptible hum of the refrigerator, the reliable heartbeat of a quiet apartment. I could write about the ache in my left knee, a souvenir from a fall I took years ago, a small, permanent footnote in the story of my body.

But those are just things. Objects and sensations. What comes to me now, as I settle into the rhythm of the keyboard, is a memory of a different kind of blankness. It was the first day of a writing workshop I took in my early twenties, full of naive ambition and a desperate hope to be seen as a “real” writer. The instructor, a wry, silver-haired man named Leo who smelled of coffee and old books, had given us the same prompt. “Write for an hour,” he’d said, tapping his watch. “No stopping. No editing. Just let it come.”

I remember the panic. The same static, the same traffic jam. For the first ten minutes, I wrote a terrible, derivative poem about the rain. Then I wrote a paragraph of a story that went nowhere, a character with no name or purpose. I could feel Leo’s presence in the room, his slow, ambling pace as he circled our tables. I was certain he would stop and look over my shoulder, see the embarrassing mess on the page, and politely suggest I consider a career in accounting. But he never did. He just walked and let us be.

And then, something shifted. I ran out of things to *try* to write. I had exhausted the beginnings of every half-baked idea I had ever had. And in that moment of giving up, something else took over. I started writing about the act of writing itself. About the pressure, the fear, the feeling of being an impostor. I wrote about the texture of the paper, the slight scratch of the pen. I wrote about the other people in the room: the woman next to me with the furious pace of someone trying to outrun a demon, the man across the table who would stop and stare at the ceiling for what felt like minutes.

And from there, a different story emerged. It wasn't a grand narrative, but a small, true one. It was about a boy who collected lost buttons. He kept them in an old mint tin, each one a mystery. He’d imagine the coats they belonged to, the people who wore them, the lives they lived. A brass button from a soldier’s uniform. A delicate glass one from a woman’s evening gown. A simple wooden toggle from a child’s duffle coat. For an hour, I lived in the world of that tin, sorting through the stories, giving each button a history. It was the most honest thing I had written in years.

When Leo called time, I felt a strange sense of loss. I had been somewhere else, a place I hadn't known existed. It was a space discovered only by running through the wall of the expected.

That’s what writing feels like to me now. It’s the process of finding that lost button. You start with the overwhelming blankness, the cacophony of choices. You try a few things that feel wrong, that are forced, that are echoes of other people's voices. And then, if you’re lucky and you’re patient, and you’re willing to be a little bored or a little scared, the noise fades. A single, quiet voice emerges. It’s not the loudest one, or the cleverest one. It’s the one that has been there all along, waiting for you to stop shouting so it could be heard.

I think about the world and its relentless demands for meaning. We are asked to have opinions, to take stands, to summarize complex realities into neat, shareable packages. We are a species obsessed with conclusions, with the tidy moral at the end of the fable. But the act of writing—the real act—is a rebellion against that. It’s a space for nuance, for ambiguity, for the exploration of a feeling without having to justify it. It’s a place where a collection of lost buttons can be as meaningful as a political treatise, because it’s a vessel for a moment of true, unadorned human attention.

So now, with 1000 words stretching out before me, I find myself back in that workshop room. The frantic static has subsided. The world has quieted down. I’m not trying to write something profound or important. I’m just trying to pay attention. To the hum of the refrigerator, the ghost of a fall, the memory of a silver-haired man and a tin of buttons. I am trying to let something come, and to trust that the act of building a bridge, one word after another, into the vast, empty space, is a meaningful thing to do, even if I don’t know where the other side will land. The space is no longer blank. It is full of everything that is, and everything that has been, and everything that just might be.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular silence in a house before anyone else wakes. It is not the absence of sound so much as the absence of obligation. The refrigerator hums. A curtain breathes against a window. Somewhere a bird repeats the same three notes as if trying to remember the fourth. I sit with a cup of coffee and the strange instruction to write a thousand words, which feels both generous and impossible, like being handed an empty room and told to fill it with weather.

The first thing that comes is not an idea but a memory: my father in the driveway, washing a car that was already clean. He had a red bucket and a sponge worn soft at the edges. He worked slowly, methodically, wringing out the water and drawing long wet arcs across the windshield. I used to think he was wasting time. Now I understand he was not washing the car. He was making a place where his mind could be still. Adults are not often allowed to do nothing, so they invent tasks that look like work and feel like prayer.

I think writing is a little like that. You sit down with a clean page and invent a task. You wring out sentences. You draw long arcs across the blankness. If you are lucky, the mind quiets and something surfaces: a question you did not know you were carrying, a name you had misplaced, a fear with a small, reasonable face.

Outside, the street is beginning to wake. A dog barks once, then thinks better of it. A car passes with the soft hiss that tires make on wet pavement, though it did not rain. I can hear the newspaper delivery person—or maybe it is someone rolling a trash bin to the curb. These small sounds are the punctuation of a neighborhood. They mark time without demanding attention.

I have been thinking lately about attention. How it is the rarest currency we have, and how we spend it in such strange ways. We give it to glowing rectangles, to arguments with strangers, to the endless refresh of things that have not changed. We withhold it from the people sitting across from us, from the sky, from our own bodies until they ache. What would it mean to be truly awake for one hour? Not productive, not optimizing, just awake: noticing the weight of a spoon in the hand, the temperature of the room, the way a thought arrives and then leaves without asking to be followed?

The coffee is getting cold. I do not mind. There is a certain honesty in cold coffee—it no longer pretends to be an event. It is just a drink. I take a sip and look at the table. The wood grain looks like a map of rivers. A crumb from yesterday’s toast sits near the edge. I decide not to wipe it away yet. It is evidence of a life being lived in small, unremarkable increments.

A thousand words is not very many. It is perhaps four pages, double-spaced. It is a long email, a short story, a half-finished argument. But a thousand words can also be a kind of architecture: a bridge from one silence to another. You place one word beside the next until you have crossed something. The trick is not to look down too often.

When I was a child, I believed that words had physical weight. I imagined “elephant” as heavy and “feather” as light, and “the” as small and gray and everywhere, like a pebble. I was disappointed to learn that words are only shapes until someone reads them. But now I think they are heavy anyway, in the way that a key is heavy because of what it opens. A single sentence can unlock a room you had boarded up years ago. It can also lock one. That is the risk of writing anything down.

I wonder about the person who will read this. Perhaps no one. Perhaps you, at this moment, drinking your own coffee or sitting on a train or waiting for water to boil. I wonder what you are carrying. What you are trying not to think about. What small, ordinary thing has been bringing you comfort lately. There is a kind of intimacy in writing to an unknown reader that feels almost unfair: I get to speak, and you get to listen, and neither of us has to worry about the awkward pause after.

The bird has found the fourth note. It repeats the whole phrase now, triumphant and slightly off-key. The house has begun to make its morning sounds: pipes ticking, floorboards settling, a phone buzzing somewhere under a cushion. The room is no longer mine alone. Soon there will be breakfast to make, questions to answer, the day’s small emergencies. I will close this page and become useful again. But not yet.

For now, I will let the words be enough. I will let the blank room fill with weather. I will let the car stay dirty. I will finish this sentence and then start another, not because I have something important to say but because the act of saying is its own small roof, and underneath it, for a little while, I am sheltered.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The thousand words begin with the hum of a library after closing. The lights are still on, but the chairs have been pushed in, and the air holds the smell of paper, dust, and rain drying on coat sleeves. I am supposed to write whatever comes to me, which is a strange instruction, because what comes first is not a thought but a feeling: the sensation of standing in a room where everyone has just left. There is a residue to silence like that. It is not empty. It is full of small evidence—a pencil on the table, a receipt used as a bookmark, a page turned down at the corner. I think about the person who left each object and wonder whether they meant to return. Most of us mean to return. Most of us do not.

Outside, the street is shining. Rain has made the asphalt into a dark mirror, and the traffic lights bleed green and red across it. A bus sighs at the corner, opens its doors, closes them, and moves on with almost no one inside. I like the city best at this hour, when it has stopped performing and has become merely itself. The bakery is shutting its shutters. The flower shop has brought its buckets inside. A man in a yellow raincoat walks a small dog that refuses to hurry. None of this is important, and that is exactly why I want to save it. The significant moments are always being photographed, but the ordinary ones are the ones that make a life feel lived.

I have been given a thousand words, and I keep thinking of all the things that cannot fit into them. A thousand words cannot hold my mother’s hands, which are smaller now than I remember and always cold in winter. It cannot hold the sound of a friend laughing on the other end of a bad telephone line, or the exact color of the sky above a parking lot in Ohio when I was nineteen and certain my life was about to begin. Words are generous and stingy at once. They let us say almost anything, but they leave a gap between what we mean and what lands on the page. We spend our lives trying to close that gap, and sometimes, for a sentence or two, we almost do.

What comes to me next is a memory of a train. I was traveling from one city to another, and a woman across the aisle was reading a book with a green cover. She read with her finger moving under the lines, as if she were keeping time. Every few pages she would stop, look out the window, and then go back to reading. I never learned her name. I never spoke to her. But I remember her more clearly than some people I have known for years. This happens, I think, because certain strangers carry a version of us we recognize. She looked the way I feel when I am reading something true: absent from the room and more present than ever.

The rain starts again, tapping the library windows with a sound like fingernails on a table. I open a book at random. It is a history of maps, and the first sentence says that every map is a lie that tells the truth. I close it again. That is how I feel about writing. We arrange events into beginnings and endings because it comforts us, even though life keeps refusing to stay in order. We leave out the hours spent waiting, the arguments about groceries, the days when nothing happens and the nothing is so heavy we mistake it for sadness. But maybe those are the real maps: the small decisions, the unremarkable afternoons, the way we choose one street over another and meet someone who changes everything.

I start to make a list of things I would put in a time capsule for no one in particular. The smell of a new box of crayons. The sound of a screen door slamming. A train ticket with the edge torn. The phrase “I’ll be right back.” A recipe card in someone else’s handwriting. The first cold day of autumn, when you wear a sweater and immediately regret it by noon. A song that reminds you of a summer you did not appreciate enough. A library book returned late. A glass of water brought to you when you did not ask. The list grows until it becomes a kind of prayer, though I am not sure to whom. Maybe gratitude is just attention paid twice.

The librarian returns from the back office and looks at the clock. It is almost time. She does not tell me to leave, but she begins turning off the lights in sections, and the room goes darker in stages, like a sentence being revised. I gather my things. On my way out, I pass the display table where the staff have arranged books about weather. I pick one up and put it back. I have enough to carry already. In the doorway, the cool air hits my face. The street is still shining. The man with the dog is gone. The bakery is dark. I stand under the awning for a moment, not wanting to step into the rain and not wanting to stay.

This is where the thousand words end, though nothing really ends here. Tomorrow the library will open again. Someone will turn down a page. Someone will forget a receipt. Someone will read a sentence that changes the shape of their day. I will probably write about something else. But for now, the rain, the bus, the yellow raincoat, the green-covered book—all of it stays with me, a small city inside a single paragraph. If you asked me what I meant by any of this, I would say I meant only to pay attention, and to leave a light on for whatever comes next.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning arrived like a quiet argument between light and fog. I opened the window and the city breathed in, smelling of rain on hot pavement, coffee, diesel, and something green trying to grow between cracks. A pigeon landed on the sill, looked at me with the confidence of someone who had paid rent, and then flew away. I made tea I did not drink. I listened to the kettle tick as it cooled. Somewhere a bus groaned, a child laughed, a door closed. The day began without asking whether any of us were ready. Not even remotely. Truly. Anyway.

At noon I walked to the market because the walls of my room had started to hum with unfinished thoughts. Vendors called out prices in languages I almost understood. Tomatoes glistened under a canvas awning. A woman with silver braids sold honey from jars labeled with handwritten names: Summer, Wildflower, Late August. I bought one called Almost Morning. She told me to keep it out of sunlight and to stir it when I felt impatient. I asked why. She said honey remembers every flower it ever loved. I believed her for exactly seven seconds, then I believed her forever. Honestly.

In the afternoon, a stray dog followed me home and then refused to enter the building. It sat on the steps like a small, dusty philosopher and watched the street. I sat beside it. We observed a man carrying three umbrellas, none open. We watched two teenagers practice a dance routine beside a parked car. We saw a cloud shaped like a spoon dissolve into a cloud shaped like nothing. The dog sighed. I sighed back. There was no wind, but leaves moved. I decided this meant something. When I stood, the dog wagged its tail once and quietly left.

By evening, I remembered a sentence from a book I had never finished: We are all weather. It felt true in the way that unfamiliar songs feel familiar. I put the honey on the windowsill, forgot the warning, and watched the setting sun turn the jar into stained glass. For a moment the kitchen was a cathedral for no god in particular. The refrigerator hummed a bass line. A spoon rested on a saucer like a question mark. I opened the book again, read the first page, and closed it. Some books are doors. Some are windows. Some are books.

I ate dinner: bread, olives, a peach. The phone rang twice and I let it. Outside, the streetlights flickered on one by one, as if the city were counting itself. I thought about the dog, the honey woman, the man with three umbrellas. Everyone was carrying something unnecessary, and maybe that was the point. We practice holding things until we learn how to put them down. We buy umbrellas for weather that never comes. We name honey after mornings we cannot keep. I washed one plate, dried one cup, and left the rest for tomorrow. Tomorrow could use a task.

That night I dreamed the city was a library and every building was a book. I walked down a street called Marginalia. The bakery held a chapter on patience. The laundromat smelled of endings. In the dream I had a library card made from pressed flowers. The librarian was the stray dog, wearing glasses and a serious expression. It stamped my hand with a date I could not read. I woke with my hand curled around nothing. The room was dark. The honey jar glowed faintly on the sill. I remembered the warning and moved it into the cupboard. Quietly.

The next morning, I wrote a list of things I did not need to do. It was surprisingly long: worry before breakfast, explain myself to strangers, solve problems that belonged to other people, rehearse conversations I would never have, apologize for taking up space, treat rest as a reward instead of a requirement. I folded the list and put it in my pocket. At the coffee shop, the barista drew a leaf in the foam. I did not tell her it looked like a comma. I thought it might be punctuation for the day, a pause placed before the clause.

At the market again, the honey woman asked if I had stirred the jar. I admitted I had forgotten. She nodded as if this were the correct answer. Forgetfulness is part of the recipe, she said. I asked what the other parts were. She counted on her fingers: sunlight, patience, bees, luck, a little fear. Fear? I asked. She smiled. Bees do not make honey for us. They make it because they are bees. We just happen to be nearby with jars. I bought another jar, this one called First Frost. She warned me it would be sharper. Very sharp.

Winter did arrive eventually, though not in any dramatic way. It came as a draft under the door, a gray morning, a coat I had forgotten I owned. I stirred the honey with a clean spoon and tasted it. Sharper, yes, but also brighter, as if the flowers had learned something from the cold. I thought about how many things improve by being left alone: soup, gardens, apologies, certain kinds of silence. I made toast. I opened the window for exactly one minute. The air bit my face and then let go. I closed the window. Winter stayed outside, then.

Tonight I am writing this because the day keeps trying to escape. Already the pigeon, the peach, the dream librarian are fading. The honey jar sits in the cupboard, heavier than before. I have not solved anything. I have not become a better person, though I did move a jar out of sunlight. Maybe that counts. Maybe goodness is mostly small corrections made without ceremony. I will wash the spoon. I will set out a cup for morning. I will leave the window open a crack so the city can breathe in. Tomorrow, if it asks, I might say yes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a peculiar kind of freedom in being told to write whatever comes to you. It is not the freedom of a wide-open field exactly; it is the freedom of a field with a fence around it, and someone has said, “Go anywhere, but stay inside the fence.” A thousand words is the fence. Or perhaps it is the field. The constraint makes the openness possible. Without a limit, the mind wanders into the fog and sits down. With a limit, it starts walking.

I think about the first sentence. It always pretends to be a beginning, but it is usually the middle of something. Even now, this thought has parents and grandparents, old conversations, half-read books, a screen at midnight, a cup of tea going cold. The first sentence is a door painted on a wall. You walk through it anyway, because what else are you going to do with a door?

Somewhere outside, a car passes. The sound is a soft tear in the evening. A dog answers it, then decides it has done its duty. There is a mosquito in the room that has been avoiding me with great skill. It is a small reminder that I am not only a mind; I am a body, a warm surface, a thing that can be bitten. All day I have been thinking in paragraphs, but the mosquito thinks in blood. Who is more honest?

I once knew a man who collected words. Not in a notebook, not in a dictionary, but in the way he talked. He would use an old-fashioned word like *gossamer* and then look around as if he had released a bird. He liked *crepuscular*. He liked *susurrus*. He said, “There are words that feel like they were made for the inside of a mouth.” I asked him what he meant. He said, “Say *luminous*. Now say *grief*. They use different parts of the tongue. They leave different aftertastes.” I have never forgotten that. I don’t know if it is true, but I know it is useful. It makes language feel less like a tool and more like a place.

A thousand words is not very long. It is a short story that ends before you know the characters’ middle names. It is an essay that has to choose one argument and defend it with only three examples. It is roughly the length of a long voicemail from someone who has missed you. It is enough to say something true, but not enough to say everything true. That is probably good for me. I am prone to saying everything true and ending up with nothing said.

What comes to me now is the image of a boy standing at the edge of a swimming pool with his toes curled over the rough concrete. The water is very blue. The sun is very bright. He is not afraid of drowning exactly; he is afraid of the cold shock, the first second when the body says *no* before it says *yes*. He jumps anyway. That is what writing is like. You stand at the edge of the blank page, and the first sentence is cold. After that you are in it.

There is something I have been meaning to write about: the way ordinary things become precious when you describe them slowly. A spoon on a table. A bus ticket with a crease down the middle. The sound of a neighbor’s television through a wall. If you look at them long enough, they stop being ordinary. A spoon is a small silver boat. A bus ticket is a receipt for a journey you may not remember making. The neighbor’s television is a distant party you were not invited to. This is not a lie. It is just a different kind of attention.

Attention is the whole game. I think that is what I actually believe. Not that writing is about cleverness, or beauty, or even truth exactly. It is about attention. The world is full of things that are happening at the same time, and most of them are asking, very quietly, to be noticed. A cloud changes shape. A person says *anyway* and means something else. A child holds a crayon with their whole fist. If you pay attention, the ordinary becomes strange, and the strange becomes ordinary, and somewhere in that swing back and forth, a sentence is born.

I wonder what I would write if I had only ten words. Probably something like: *I was here. I noticed. I am still listening.* That is not a story, but it is a start. With a hundred words, I might describe the rain. With a thousand, I can have opinions about rain. I can say that rain is not romantic, but the idea of rain is; that real rain is cold and inconvenient and smells like pavement; that the romance is in the shelter, in the decision to stay inside and watch it, in the tea, in the window, in the feeling of being spared.

There is a spider outside the window. It has built a web between the sill and the frame, and it sits in the middle like a tiny punctuation mark. I don’t know what punctuation it would be. A period, probably. A full stop with legs. It has been there for two days. I have not seen it catch anything. I want to tell it that the location is poor, that the traffic is low, that it should try the other side of the window. But I am not a spider, and perhaps the traffic is invisible to me. Perhaps there are whole economies of small winged things happening at dawn. This is what I mean about attention. You look at a spider and suddenly the world is larger.

I am running out of words, which is the point. The page is no longer empty. It has footprints. We have been here for a thousand words. Time to notice something else.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The box was on the top shelf of the closet, behind a folded blanket and a jar of coins from countries that no longer existed. It was not a mysterious box. It was cardboard, soft at the corners, smelling faintly of dust and old rain. Inside were photographs with no names on the back. People standing in front of cars, people squinting into sun, a woman holding a cake as if it were a sleeping bird. I did not recognize any of them. For a long time I sat on the floor and tried to invent their lives, because a photograph without a story is a door with no house behind it.

One photograph showed a man in a pale suit standing beside a river. He held his hat in both hands, not as though he had just taken it off but as though he was offering it to the water. Behind him, a bridge crossed nothing I could identify. The sky was the color of cheap paper. I imagined he was waiting for someone who had promised to meet him at noon but had already decided, somewhere across the city, not to come. I imagined he knew this and stayed anyway, because waiting can be a kind of dignity. The photograph did not tell me whether he ever crossed the bridge. It only kept him there, suspended in the moment before leaving.

Another showed three children on a porch, arranged by height. The smallest held a stick like a scepter. The tallest had her hand on his shoulder, a gesture that might have been comfort or correction. They were all laughing at something outside the frame—someone behind the camera, perhaps, making a face. I liked this photograph because it had no tragedy in it. Not every old picture needs to become a ghost story. Sometimes a summer afternoon is just a summer afternoon, and the people in it are simply warm and alive and squinting against the light. The present is always disappearing, but it does not always leave a wound.

On the back of one photograph, in pencil almost rubbed away, someone had written: “After the storm, 1963.” The image itself showed a street covered in branches. A dog stood in the middle of the road, facing away from the camera, as if guarding the damage. The houses looked ordinary and stubborn. I wondered who had written the note, whether they had survived the storm, whether they were the kind of person who labeled things to keep from losing them. I am that kind of person. I write dates on folders and names on boxes. I believe memory is a shelf, and if I label everything correctly, nothing will fall.

But memory is not a shelf. It is a river with a habit of changing its bed. The photographs were proof: strangers preserved in moments that no longer belonged to anyone. Someone had kept them for decades, then forgotten them, then died, then left them to a house, then the house to me. I felt an odd responsibility. Not to identify them—I never would—but to acknowledge them. To look carefully. To say, silently: I see your hat, your cake, your dog in the road. I do not know your names, but you were here, and the light fell on you, and someone loved you enough to point a camera.

I put the photographs back in the box, but I did not return the box to the shelf. I left it on the table for a week. Every morning I passed it and thought, I should do something with that. Every evening I passed it again and thought, tomorrow. On the eighth day I opened it and chose one photograph—the man by the river—and slipped it into a book. I do not know why that one. Maybe because he looked like he was waiting, and I understand waiting. Maybe because the river was the only thing in the picture that was still moving, even after all those years, in the imagination of anyone who looked.

The book was a dictionary. I thought that was funny in a quiet way: an unnamed man hidden inside the definition of words, none of which could explain him. When I opened the dictionary weeks later, the photograph had shifted and was now marking the page for “threshold.” I decided not to move it. If a photograph can choose a word, who am I to argue? Threshold: the sill of a door; the entrance; the point of beginning. It seemed right for a man standing beside a river with his hat in his hands. Every crossing begins with someone standing still.

That night I dreamed of the box. It was full of keys, not photographs, and each key had a paper tag with a word on it: almost, afterward, home, enough, forgive. I tried one in a door that appeared in the middle of a field. The door opened onto the same field. I tried another key and it opened onto a kitchen I had never seen, where someone was making tea. I woke before I could thank them. The dream did not feel like a message. It felt like a mood, the way a house can feel like a mood. I lay in the dark and listened to the refrigerator hum.

In the morning, I labeled the box after all. On a scrap of paper I wrote: “Photographs, unknown, found in closet.” Then I crossed out “unknown” and wrote “unclaimed.” Then I crossed out “unclaimed” and left it blank. Some things do not want a name. They want only to be kept, the way a stone in a pocket is kept, not for its use but for the small weight of it. I put the box back on the shelf, behind the blanket, beside the jar of foreign coins. It is still there. Sometimes I think of the man by the river, still waiting in the dictionary at “threshold,” and I hope someone came. I hope the light changed. I hope he put his hat back on and walked.

Not every story needs to be solved. Some just need a witness, a quiet room, and a person willing to say: I remember you, even though I never knew you. That is enough. That is often enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Museum of Small Things

This morning I found a receipt in the pocket of a winter coat: one orange, one loaf of bread, a candle shaped like a pear. The date had faded into a blue smudge, but I remembered the day anyway—or thought I did. Memory is a poor archivist. It keeps the ticket stub and loses the film. Still, I stood by the window with the receipt in my hand and felt the whole afternoon come back: the cold air sharp as a clean knife, the bakery steaming like a small, honest engine, the candle that never got lit because it looked too much like a fruit to burn.

I have been thinking about small things lately. Not small in the sense of unimportant, but small in the sense that they fit in the palm. A key. A stone. A sentence someone says and then forgets. The way a stranger on the bus held her umbrella with both hands as if it might try to escape. These are the objects and gestures that make up a life, though we rarely put them on display. We save the big moments in albums and the little ones in our bodies, where they wait like seeds.

On my walk to the corner store, I passed a man watering a single plant in a cracked pot. He was very serious about it. The water fell in a thin silver thread, and the plant—some kind of fern, maybe—looked no better or worse for the attention. But the man’s face had the concentration of a watchmaker. I wanted to tell him that I understood. That sometimes the only way to keep the world from spinning too fast is to water one small thing and watch the water disappear into the dirt.

The corner store smelled of cardboard and oranges. The woman behind the counter was reading a paperback with a broken spine. She didn’t look up when I came in, and I appreciated that. There is a kind of trust in not being watched. I bought milk and a chocolate bar I didn’t need and a lemon because it was the color of a good mood. Outside, the sky was doing that thing it does in early spring—gray, then silver, then almost blue—as if it can’t decide whether to apologize or start over.

I used to think that meaning arrived in loud rooms. Now I think it arrives in kitchens at night, when the dishwasher is humming and someone has left a spoon on the counter and the clock is ticking like a small, patient animal. My mother used to leave her teacup in the sink with a little tea still in it. I would find it in the morning, a dark ring at the bottom, and know she had been there, awake before me, thinking her private thoughts. That ring was a kind of message. Not a sentence, exactly. More like a proof of presence.

There is a word I like: “petrichor.” The smell of rain on dry ground. I like it not because it is beautiful—though it is—but because it names something we would otherwise have to point at and say, “You know, that smell.” Language is full of these small rescues. It reaches down and pulls a feeling out of the mud and gives it a little name tag. Most of the time we forget the names. But sometimes, on a walk, the air changes, and the word surfaces like a fish, and for a second the world is more specific than it was before.

At the end of my street there is a bench that nobody sits on. It faces a wall. I have decided it is a bench for thinking about walls. Once I saw a pigeon land on its back and stay there for a long time, doing nothing. Pigeons are excellent at doing nothing. They have mastered the art of being a small gray thought in a loud city. I envy them a little. I envy anyone who can sit still without feeling that stillness is a debt they will have to pay back later.

Tonight I will make soup. I will chop an onion and cry, and it will be a small, ordinary ceremony. I will listen to the radio and miss half of what is said and think about the receipt in my pocket and the man watering his fern and the woman with her paperback and the lemon on the counter, bright as a tiny sun. The world will keep doing what it does—breaking and mending, forgetting and remembering—and I will be here, in the middle of it, paying attention to the small things. Not because they are all I can manage. Because they are, in the end, the things that hold the whole thing together. A key. A stone. A sentence. A candle shaped like a pear.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular hour before a city wakes when it belongs to no one. The streetlights still burn, but they’ve lost their confidence; the sky has gone gray at the edges, and the first buses move like enormous, patient animals. I have always loved that hour, though I rarely see it honestly—usually I meet it from the wrong side, still awake instead of newly risen, with the taste of midnight in my mouth and unfinished thoughts scattered around me. Still, it feels like a secret: the bakery with its lights on but the door locked, a man hosing down the pavement, a pigeon inspecting a discarded crust as if it were a small archaeological site. The city is not asleep. It is simply unmade. For a little while, everything is possible because nothing has begun.

I think about memory the way some people think about weather. It arrives without permission, changes the temperature of a room, leaves tracks on the windows. I remember my grandmother’s kitchen not as a room but as a set of sounds: the click of the gas burner, the radio murmuring in a language I only half understood, a spoon circling a cup of tea. She used to say that patience was a form of intelligence. I didn’t know what she meant then. I thought intelligence was the crossword puzzle, the recall of capital cities, the ability to win arguments. Now I suspect she meant the kind of attention that doesn’t rush to convert the world into a conclusion. Patience as a way of staying inside the question. A kind of intelligence that knows when not to speak.

Lately I’ve been trying to notice the things that don’t announce themselves. The way a friend’s voice softens when he talks about his daughter. The crack in the sidewalk that a weed has mistaken for an address. The way a sentence can carry someone’s whole history in the pause before the last word. We are trained, I think, to look for the loud evidence: the promotion, the announcement, the milestone. But most of a life is made of unphotographed afternoons. The sandwiches. The waiting rooms. The conversations that go nowhere and mean everything. If someone wanted to understand me, they would need the unglamorous data: the books I’ve abandoned, the apologies I rehearsed and never delivered, the songs I play when I’m not trying to feel anything in particular.

In the evenings, I walk without a destination. This is one of the few habits I have kept from childhood. My mother used to say I walked like a person looking for a place to put a thought. She was not wrong. Movement helps me locate what I’m thinking, as if the thought were a small object rattling around in my pocket, and walking shakes it loose. On these walks I pass the same houses, the same dogs, the same corner where the streetlight flickers in a way that no one has bothered to fix. I have invented biographies for the people behind the lit windows. The man with the upright piano who plays the same eight bars, badly and passionately, at ten o’clock. The woman who waters plants on a balcony in the rain. The child who jumps on a couch while an adult’s shadow gestures from the kitchen. I know these stories are probably false. But they are also true in the way that all imagined lives are true: they remind me that every window is a world, and every world is mostly hidden.

Sometimes I worry that we are losing the ability to be bored. Boredom is not the same as emptiness. Boredom is a threshold, and if you stand on it long enough, something strange and necessary begins to speak. A memory, a question, a ridiculous idea. The mind wanders off and returns with a flower in its teeth. Now we have filled every gap with noise. We reach for a screen while the kettle boils, while the elevator climbs, while the person across from us gathers the courage to say something true. I am not innocent. I am as reachable as anyone. But I’ve started leaving small silences around my day like bowls of water for the birds. I don’t always know what they’re for. I only know that when I return, they are sometimes empty.

What I want, I think, is not a bigger life but a more inhabited one. I want to be present in the room I am actually in, with the people who are actually here, doing the work that is actually in front of me. This sounds simple and is not. The mind is a tourist with a terrible sense of direction. It goes to the past and starts rearranging the furniture. It goes to the future and buys things it doesn’t need. It turns a small disagreement into a courtroom, a stray comment into a verdict. But every so often, through effort or accident, the tourist comes home. The room becomes vivid. The cup is warm in your hand. Someone laughs and you hear it fully, not as background but as a fact. These moments don’t last, and perhaps they shouldn’t. But they are enough to suggest that life is not a problem to be solved. It is a place to be lived in, imperfectly, with attention.

The sky is fully light now. The buses have become crowded, the bakery door is open, and the city has made up its mind about the day. I can hear a distant siren, a door slamming, the first argument of the morning. I should sleep, or eat something, or answer messages. But I want to hold on to the hour before waking just a little longer—that hour when the world was gray and unfinished and anything could happen. Then again, something is always about to happen. That is the terror and the gift. We are not promised the whole day, only this one next breath, this next small decision: to look up, to listen, to begin again.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
What comes to me first is the sound of a refrigerator humming in an empty kitchen, that low electric ocean. It is early, the kind of early where the light hasn't decided what color it wants to be. The window is gray. A single bird is practicing the same three notes, as if it has lost the rest of the song and is too proud to ask for help. Somewhere a car passes, water hisses under its tires, and the street goes back to being a secret.

I think about how many mornings begin this way: nobody watching, nothing dramatic, just the machinery of the world keeping its promise. The coffee maker clicks. Steam curls upward like a question mark that forgets itself. I hold the warm mug and feel how ordinary miracles get, how quickly we learn to call them Tuesday.

Then the mind wanders, because minds are not loyal animals. It goes to a summer afternoon when I was ten and found a grasshopper on the sidewalk. Its legs were jointed like tiny machinery, its eyes all surface. I did not touch it. I crouched for a long time, close to the concrete, and felt the heat rise through my shoes. That was the whole event. A grasshopper, a sidewalk, a boy trying to understand the difference between looking and owning. I remember the grasshopper's color—a green so bright it seemed to have been mixed with sunlight. I remember nothing else about that day. No before, no after. Just a small green hinge in the middle of time.

Memory is strange that way. It keeps the receipts but not the purchases. It saves the smell of a school hallway, the squeak of a gym floor, the exact way a friend's jacket looked when they turned to wave from a bus. It drops whole years into a pocket and then pats the wrong pocket. We build ourselves out of these scraps and call it a life.

The bird outside tries again. Three notes, then a pause, then the same three notes. For a moment I imagine the pause is the important part. Not the song, but the space where the song might change. We are always waiting for the next note. We are always certain we know what it will be.
